lines.text: The shell runs one job by hand.
A pipeline runs the same commands on every change. It stops at the first failure.
This refresher covers the loop around it: review, tests, continuous integration, version numbers, and pinned dependencies. The strip along the top marks where each step sits.
All familiar? Swipe on.
A review has an order... design first, and style last.
Take the broad view first. Then the design of the main part; if something big is wrong, say so right away.
Then functionality, complexity, tests, and naming. Style is only a nit the author may skip.
Approve when the change clearly improves the code... not when it's perfect.
Keep pull requests small. About a hundred lines is reasonable. A thousand is usually too large.
And answer within one business day.
Now a unit test: the bisect oracle from the Git refresher, grown up.
One test, parametrized: one case per input, each passing or failing on its own.
A fixture hands each test its own fresh temporary folder.
But does it fail when the code is broken?
Six tests run. Four cases, the Git oracle, and a test of the main function.
At that commit, four tests fail. The two that pass have no stray spaces.
The run exits with one... and the gate closes.
A job on the runner is a script that stops on error. Each step runs only if the one before it succeeded.
Each step is a new shell, and its exit status is its verdict.
The first non-zero status fails the job... and every step after it is skipped.
On the left, the fix goes green.
On the right, the regression stops at the tests. The diff step never runs.
Make the job a required check, and a red run blocks the merge.
Here's the trap from the shell refresher, now on a runner.
This step sets no shell, so GitHub runs bash with stop-on-error. The first command can't open the file and fails; the other two succeed.
So... does the step pass, or fail?
It passes. Stop-on-error sees only a pipeline's last command... zero.
The failure is hidden, in any script, not just on a runner.
Ask for bash explicitly, pipe-fail switches on, and the step fails, as it should.
A flaky test passes and fails on the same code.
Here, the test compared the order of a set. That order isn't specified. For strings it depends on a hash value, and Python picks a different seed in every process.
Run it twenty times, and half the runs fail.
Re-running until it's green hides the problem. And a gate nobody trusts hides real failures, too.
Fix the cause. Here... sort first.
A version number is a promise about what callers can rely on.
The library is at version one point five. A fix bumps the last number; a compatible addition, the middle one.
Now the next release renames an output column. Which version is it?
Version two. Every reader of the old column breaks.
The first number goes up, and the other two reset to zero.
And a released version never changes, so you can't rebuild one point five.
For data, a rename isn't the only break: a new status value, a changed type, even an extra column.
Works on my machine.
The requirements file says the library, version one point four or later.
Your laptop installed one point five last week. Today, version two is published, with the renamed column.
What does a brand new run start with?
It gets version two... and the app fails with a missing-key error.
Or later admits every later version, and pip takes the newest.
The application should pin exactly, with a lock: next step.
For a library, always set a lower bound. Set a cap only for a known break.
A lock file freezes the tree.
An application pins every package with an exact version and a checksum of the exact file, the same on every machine.
A lock tool writes those lines, not you.
With hash checking on, pip installs those bytes... or nothing.
If a file changes under a pinned version, the checksum fails, and pip refuses.
A lock guarantees the same install, wherever it fits. Not that it's correct.
Eight things to keep.
Review design first, in small changes. Tests must fail on the bug.
The runner stops at the first non-zero exit. Explicit bash adds the pipe fail option. Flaky tests need their state fixed.
Versions: fix, add, or break. Applications pin, with a lock. Libraries set a lower bound, and cap only a known break.
The gate checks the answer... not what it costs as the data grows.
Next up... the last of the five refreshers: the notation for that, and the logarithms the chapter counts with.
